newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE-Malaysia car tycoon faces wrath over buses.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Malaysia car tycoon faces wrath over buses.

text.p: Malaysian transport tycoon Yahaya Ahmad made international news last October when he bought British sportscar maker Group Lotus Ltd.
The respected automotive engineer, dubbed the "car czar" in Malaysia, controls a big chunk of the domestic transport business through carmaker Proton Bhd.
Yahaya also owns vehicle assemblers and a plant which turns out Malaysia's homemade motorcycle, the Kriss.
But in the last few weeks, Yahaya has had to deal with a more pedestrian pursuit -- trying to run Kuala Lumpur's chaotic bus system efficiently.
Hit by a wave of public anger, Yahaya rode around on a Kriss earlier this month trying to improve the services of buses operated by his firm Intrakota Consolidated Sdn Bhd.
The 50-year-old Yahaya rode his motorbike from one bus station to another trying to smoothen the services and ruffled feathers of Kuala Lumpur's bus commuters.

"I will not run away from this responsibility. It is a big responsibility and even the Prime Minister (Mahathir Mohamad) himself has directed that the problems be sorted out," Yahaya said in an interview with Bernama, the national news agency.
The government on January 1 removed from the streets the services of most of the 800 mini-buses operated by small businessmen. It also ended the public bus services of S.J. Kenderaan Sdn Bhd.
The long-planned moves were part of a strategy to better manage public transportation in the city and the Klang Valley area which surrounds Kuala Lumpur.
GOVERNMENT KEEN TO IMPROVE TRANSPORT BEFORE 1998 GAMES
The city of two million will play host to the 1998 Commonwealth Games and the government has been trying to spruce up its public transportation.
Late last year, it began a crackdown on wayward taxi drivers, ordering them to wear uniforms and banning vehicles older than seven years.
In December, Kuala Lumpur launched the first of four above-ground commuter rail systems.

Operators of the notorious pink mini-buses took their fair share of deserved grief from the public for blatantly breaking traffic rules, intimidating passengers and motorists, and simply avoiding stops on traffic-clogged routes.
But Intrakota, with its smartly-capped uniformed drivers and scheduled runs, has not been able to immediately fill in the gaps left by the mini-buses and S.J. Kenderaan.
Fickle commuters yearned for the anarchic but nimble pink buses when they found that Intrakota's 500 vehicles were strictly following schedules, route stops and traffic rules.
The issue was quickly picked up by newspapers and radio and television talk shows.
Red-faced Intrakota executives added to the anger when they said in early January that services will only be improved in February.
Yahaya then got involved personally. He also said Malaysians needed to adopt a new bus "culture".
"The mini-bus service operates like a taxi. It does not have schedules. It has routes but does not follow the routes.
"Intrakota cannot, and in fact, is not allowed to do so. Our buses move according to schedules and assigned routes and cannot simply enter any roads," Yahaya told Bernama.
INTRAKOTA PLANS MORE BUSES, AD CAMPAIGNS
Earlier this week, a vehicle assembly firm owned by Yahaya said it was working hard to produce more buses for Intrakota.
Intrakota is also running big advertisements in newspapers showing pictures of nine commuters singing the praises of the company's bus services.
The government has also promised to make special bus lanes in the city.
Analysts said Intrakota's problems are a manifestation of Malaysia's economic boom and the nation's successful car-making projects.
Eight years of eight percent growth or better and the relatively cheap cars produced by Yahaya's Proton plants have made driving in the city a slow-motion experience.
Cars made by Proton and a unit of Yahaya's Diversified Resources Bhd accounted for 80 percent of new cars sold in the country in the last few years.
Yahaya will have to balance his hopes of selling more Protons with that of serving the bus-commuting public more efficiently, analysts said.
